title: Green v. Commissioner
subject: Trade or Business Requirement for Passive Research-Funding Partnerships
summary: Green v. Commissioner, 83 T.C. 667 (1984), is the U.S. Tax Court decision holding that R&D expenditures qualify under IRC § 174 only if incurred in connection with the taxpayer's own trade or business. It applies to R&D partnerships and investors; LaSala, Ltd. lost its deductions because its same-day exclusive license to NPDC was treated as a sale.

body.text: 1. Executive Summary & Case Background
Procedural Posture and Factual Architecture of LaSala, Ltd.

In the jurisprudence governing United States federal research and development (R&D) tax incentives, Green v. Commissioner, 83 T.C. 667 (1984), stands as the foundational United States Tax Court decision delineating the boundary between a bona fide research-conducting enterprise and a passive investment vehicle. The litigation arose from a statutory notice of deficiency issued by the Commissioner of Internal Revenue determining deficiencies of $32,582.29 for 1979 and $38,508.63 for 1980 (plus additions to tax under section 6653(a)) against petitioners Harold J. Green and Marion F. Green, husband and wife, after disallowing the partnership losses they claimed by reason of Mr. Green's investment as a limited partner in LaSala, Ltd. ("LaSala"), an Illinois limited partnership organized on December 29, 1977, and reorganized and expanded on December 19, 1979 (83 T.C. at 668–669).

LaSala was reorganized with the stated purpose of acquiring four inventions for investment and income-producing purposes and thereafter patenting, improving, maintaining, and exploiting the inventions; its new general partner, Tower Hill Co., Inc., had been incorporated only on November 30, 1979, and had no previous experience in the acquisition and exploitation of inventions (83 T.C. at 668–670). On or about December 24, 1979, shortly after its reorganization, LaSala entered into four sets of agreements, one set for each invention, with each set comprising three interlocking contracts entered into on the same day: an acquisition agreement, a research and development agreement, and an exclusive license agreement (83 T.C. at 670). Under four separate Acquisition Agreements, LaSala first acquired all rights, title, and interest in the four inventions from their respective inventors. Concurrently, LaSala entered into four Research and Development Agreements with National Patent Development Corporation (NPDC), a patent development company engaged in activities worldwide that had been in existence for more than 20 years and whose stock was traded on the American Stock Exchange, obligating NPDC, for fees totaling $650,000 payable in installments through October 1, 1981, to provide the research and experimental services, systems analysis, and technical documentation reasonably necessary to develop the four inventions into commercially viable, marketable products or processes (83 T.C. at 671–672). On the same day the R&D contracts were entered into, LaSala also entered into four Exclusive License Agreements with NPDC, granting NPDC the exclusive worldwide right and license to enjoy, commercialize, manufacture, use, sell, and exploit the four inventions, including all improvements, for the life of any patents issued on them, in exchange for royalties computed as declining percentages of NPDC's future net revenue and net income from the inventions, with LaSala's royalty rights terminating between April 30, 1987, and April 30, 1989 (83 T.C. at 672–676).

Operating on the accrual method of accounting, LaSala accrued and deducted the entire $650,000 obligation payable to NPDC under the four R&D agreements (fees due in 1979, 1980, and 1981, funded from the limited partners' capital contributions, which were payable in three annual installments; Mr. Green, for example, paid $15,000 in cash and gave a non-interest-bearing note of $26,250) as research and experimental expenditures on its 1979 federal partnership return pursuant to Internal Revenue Code (IRC) § 174(a)(1). LaSala also claimed depreciation (reported as amortization) deductions on a claimed $8,801,000 cost basis in the inventions, and the petitioners claimed loss deductions attributable to LaSala on their joint federal income tax returns for 1979 and 1980 (83 T.C. at 668, 676–677).
The Commissioner's Challenge and the Taxpayer's Reliance on Snow

Upon examination, the Internal Revenue Service (IRS), through the notice of deficiency and an amendment to the Commissioner's answer, disallowed the entire amount of the petitioners' LaSala loss deductions, and the Commissioner then moved for partial summary judgment under Tax Court Rule 121 with respect to the partnership's claimed depreciation and IRC § 174 deductions (83 T.C. at 668, 677). The Commissioner contended that LaSala's $650,000 R&D expenditure was not "in connection with" any "trade or business" within the meaning of IRC § 174(a)(1) because LaSala was never intended to enter into, nor financially capable of carrying on, an active trade or business, and further that the research was not carried on in LaSala's behalf because LaSala had divested itself of ownership of the inventions (83 T.C. at 684–685). In the Commissioner's view, the Exclusive License Agreements effected a sale of the inventions to NPDC on the same day LaSala acquired them, so that LaSala received no depreciable asset in return and neither used the inventions in a trade or business nor held them for the production of income; for purposes of the motion only, the Commissioner accepted as true the assertions in the documentary record and conceded that LaSala entered into the transactions with a profit motive (83 T.C. at 668, 678).

In defense of the claimed IRC § 174 deduction, the petitioners relied on the United States Supreme Court's landmark ruling in Snow v. Commissioner, 416 U.S. 500 (1974), and on Cleveland v. Commissioner, 297 F.2d 169 (4th Cir. 1961). In Snow, the Supreme Court held that a start-up limited partnership formed to develop a prototype incinerator could deduct R&D expenditures under IRC § 174(a)(1) even though the partnership had not yet manufactured or sold any product during the taxable year at issue. Relying on Snow's holding that the phrase "in connection with" a trade or business in IRC § 174 should not be limited by the more restrictive definitions of "trade or business" used for other provisions such as the "carrying on" standard of IRC § 162(a), the petitioners argued that, even if a sale of the inventions occurred in December 1979, LaSala's role with regard to the development of the inventions was sufficient to place its R&D payments to NPDC "in connection with" a trade or business, and that LaSala's interest in future royalties was itself sufficient to mean that NPDC conducted the development on LaSala's behalf (83 T.C. at 685–686). Furthermore, the petitioners contended that the successful development of the inventions was intended to be a condition precedent to the effectiveness of the license agreements (so that no same-day sale occurred), that LaSala alternatively had exchanged its patent interests for depreciable licenses, and that LaSala retained the right to control NPDC's research and exercised it in a manner sufficiently substantial and continuous to constitute a trade or business (83 T.C. at 680, 690).
Governing Statutory and Regulatory Framework

The dispute in Green v. Commissioner implicates an interconnected web of provisions within the Internal Revenue Code of 1954 (and its successor provisions in the Internal Revenue Code of 1986, as amended) alongside corresponding Treasury Regulations. At the time of the ruling (and prior to the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act of 2017 mandatory amortization amendments effective for tax years beginning after December 31, 2021, subsequently modified by domestic expensing restorations under IRC § 174A), IRC § 174(a)(1) permitted a taxpayer to elect to treat research or experimental expenditures paid or incurred during the taxable year "in connection with his trade or business" as current deductions not chargeable to a capital account. Whether expensed currently or amortized over statutory recovery periods, the threshold statutory requirement remains identical: the expenditure must be incurred in connection with the taxpayer's own trade or business.

Complementing the statute, Treasury Regulation § 1.174-2(a) defines "research or experimental expenditures" as expenditures incurred in connection with the taxpayer's trade or business which represent research and development costs in the experimental or laboratory sense, generally including all costs incident to the development or improvement of a product or pilot model. Crucially, Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(a)(2) (redesignated in modern regulations as Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(a)(10)) provides that IRC § 174 applies not only to costs paid or incurred by the taxpayer for research or experimentation undertaken directly by the taxpayer, "but also to expenditures paid or incurred for research or experimentation carried on in his behalf by another person or organization (such as a research institute, foundation, engineering company, or similar contractor)". Additionally, IRC § 174(e) and Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(a)(6) mandate that research expenditures are eligible only to the extent that the amount is reasonable under the circumstances.

The operational nexus of IRC § 174 is further informed by the general trade or business standards of IRC § 162(a) and the profit-motive limitations of IRC § 183. Under Commissioner v. Groetzinger, 480 U.S. 23 (1987), and foundational tax precedent, engaging in a "trade or business" requires that the taxpayer be involved in the activity with "continuity and regularity" and that the taxpayer's primary purpose for engaging in the activity be for income or profit. A sporadic activity, passive investment, hobby, or amusement does not qualify as a trade or business. Under IRC § 183 and Treas. Reg. § 1.183-2(b), activities not engaged in for a bona fide profit objective are disallowed beyond gross income derived from the activity.

Finally, the statutory framework of IRC § 174 directly governs eligibility for the federal R&D tax credit under IRC § 41 (Credit for Increasing Research Activities). Originally enacted in the Economic Recovery Tax Act of 1981 as IRC § 44F, renumbered as IRC § 30 in 1984, and permanently codified as IRC § 41 by the Tax Reform Act of 1986 and the Protecting Americans from Tax Hikes (PATH) Act of 2015, the federal research credit incorporates IRC § 174 directly into its threshold definition of qualified research. Under the four-part test of IRC § 41(d)(1), to constitute "qualified research," an activity must first be research "with respect to which expenditures may be treated as specified research or experimental expenditures under section 174" (the Section 174 Eligibility Test). Moreover, IRC § 41(b)(1) imposes a heightened operational nexus, restricting Qualified Research Expenses (QREs)—comprising in-house wages, supplies, computer leasing, and 65% of eligible contract research expenses—to amounts paid or incurred by the taxpayer "in carrying on any trade or business of the taxpayer". In addition, IRC § 41(d)(4)(H) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d) exclude "funded research" where the taxpayer fails to retain "substantial rights" in the research results.
The Tax Court's Final Holding and the Post-Snow Doctrinal Shift

In an opinion by Judge Simpson filed November 5, 1984, that became the bedrock of federal R&D tax litigation, the United States Tax Court granted the Commissioner's motion for partial summary judgment, holding that the petitioners were not entitled to deduct any partnership losses for 1979 and 1980 attributable to the depreciation claimed on the four inventions or attributable to the IRC § 174 deduction claimed for 1979 (83 T.C. at 667, 691). The Tax Court systematically dismantled the petitioner's expansive reading of Snow v. Commissioner. Writing for the Court, Judge Simpson explained that while Snow relieved start-up enterprises of the obligation to have an active, revenue-producing business in the exact year R&D costs are incurred, Snow "did not eliminate the 'trade or business' requirement of section 174 altogether". The Court established the definitive two-pronged doctrinal standard governing IRC § 174 eligibility, holding that for IRC § 174 to apply, "the taxpayer must still be engaged in a trade or business at some time, and we must still determine, through an examination of the facts of each case, whether the taxpayer's activities in connection with a product are sufficiently substantial and regular to constitute a trade or business for purposes of such section" (Green v. Commissioner, 83 T.C. at 686–687).

Applying this standard to LaSala's contractual arrangements, the Tax Court held that the license agreements effected a sale of the inventions to NPDC on the same day LaSala acquired them, that LaSala's activities never surpassed those of an investor, and that LaSala itself would never be able to produce or market the inventions because of the exclusiveness of NPDC's license (83 T.C. at 681–682, 687–688). Because LaSala divested itself of all production, manufacturing, and marketing rights to the four inventions via the simultaneous Exclusive License Agreements with NPDC on the very day it acquired the inventions, the Court concluded that LaSala functioned only as a vehicle for injecting risk capital into the development and commercialization of the four inventions and was not the up-and-coming business that IRC § 174 is intended to promote (83 T.C. at 687).
2. Core Legal & Evidentiary Failures

The disqualification of the claimed R&D deductions in Green v. Commissioner was not the result of a single isolated oversight, but rather a systemic failure of transactional substance, contractual drafting, and operational governance. A rigorous legal and technical dissection of the opinion reveals four interlocking deficiencies that proved fatal to the taxpayer's claim, together with a fifth, derivative consequence for the IRC § 41 research credit (which was not at issue in Green), and these continue to inform IRS examinations under both IRC § 174 and IRC § 41.
Simultaneous Divestiture of Substantial Rights via Pre-Wired Exclusive Licensing

The central legal failure in Green stemmed from the partnership's immediate surrender of commercial ownership over the subject technologies. The petitioners argued that the parties intended the successful development of the inventions to be a condition precedent to the effectiveness of the license agreements, so that LaSala did not sell the inventions on the same day it acquired them, and alternatively that LaSala had exchanged its patent interests for "licenses" constituting depreciable intangible assets (83 T.C. at 680).

The Tax Court rejected these contentions by scrutinizing the temporal and legal mechanics of the Exclusive License Agreements. Finding the license agreements unambiguous, the Court held that their operative provisions (the present grant of the license, its coverage of improvements LaSala then owned or thereafter acquired, royalty percentages fixed for 1979 and 1980, limits on termination before January 1, 1982, and NPDC's undertaking to commercialize the products immediately upon execution) made them effective immediately, and that because LaSala retained no power to supervise, review, or direct NPDC's work, development was not a condition precedent to the licenses (83 T.C. at 681–683). LaSala thus acquired four specific inventions and, in a prearranged, simultaneous closing on the same day it engaged NPDC to develop them, granted NPDC an immediately effective, worldwide exclusive license for the life of any patents on the inventions, subject only to limited termination rights (such as NPDC's right to terminate after January 1, 1982, if annual royalties fell below $15,000, and LaSala's right to terminate upon NPDC's default) (83 T.C. at 675, 681–682).

Under established federal tax principles governing intellectual property transfers, derived from the Supreme Court's patent law decision in Waterman v. MacKenzie, 138 U.S. 252 (1891), and consistent with the "all substantial rights" standard of IRC § 1235, the grant, for consideration, of an exclusive right to make, use, and sell an invention for the duration of the patent term constitutes a sale or assignment of the grantor's substantial rights rather than a mere license, whether the consideration is a lump sum, installments of a fixed sum, or royalties based on use or sales; the petitioners did not contest this principle (83 T.C. at 679–680, 683–684). As the Tax Court held, LaSala, through the appropriate terms of art, unequivocally conveyed to NPDC all of its substantial rights in the four inventions on the day it acquired them (83 T.C. at 679–680); the Seventh Circuit later described the Green partnership as one that "released, by contract, all of the normal attributes of an R & D venture" (Levin v. Commissioner, 832 F.2d 403 (7th Cir. 1987)), and, in an unpublished order adopting a Tax Court opinion in Goulding v. Commissioner, 928 F.2d 1135 (7th Cir. 1991), applied similar reasoning to a different partnership that had "effectively sold all its interest" in its technology to its contractor. Having disposed of its working interest in the technologies immediately upon acquisition, LaSala possessed no intellectual property left to exploit in a future trade or business of its own.
Absence of Operational Capability and the "Realistic Prospect" Standard

A second fatal deficiency in Green was that, because of the exclusiveness of NPDC's license, LaSala itself would never be able to produce or market the inventions, and nothing indicated that LaSala intended to buy and sell inventions for profit on a regular basis (83 T.C. at 688–689). The Tax Court noted that LaSala itself did not conduct any research or experimentation, that LaSala and its general partner, Tower Hill, had no history as a trade or business, and that LaSala's activities after December 1979 were purely ministerial (83 T.C. at 670, 688). According to the projections in the partnership's Confidential Private Offering Memorandum, LaSala's entire capital of $1,376,000 was to be expended within its first 25 months of operation: $650,000 for research and development, $37,500 for invention acquisition installments, and the balance for the general partner's management and organization fees, legal, accounting, and offeree representative fees, and miscellaneous costs (83 T.C. at 669).

In the appellate decisions that built on Green, such as Spellman v. Commissioner, 845 F.2d 148 (7th Cir. 1988), Zink v. United States, 929 F.2d 1015 (5th Cir. 1991), Diamond v. Commissioner, 930 F.2d 372 (4th Cir. 1991), Harris v. Commissioner, 16 F.3d 75 (5th Cir. 1994), and Kantor v. Commissioner, 998 F.2d 1514 (9th Cir. 1993), the federal courts synthesized this failure into the "Realistic Prospect" test, a formulation that does not itself appear in the Green opinion. To satisfy IRC § 174 when a taxpayer is not yet actively selling goods or services, the taxpayer must demonstrate a realistic prospect of subsequently entering into its own trade or business utilizing the fruits of the research. While the probability of a firm entering into its own business satisfies IRC § 174, the mere legal possibility or hypothetical entitlement to do so does not.

Demonstrating a realistic prospect requires proving two conjunctive elements during the tax years at issue: objective intent and practical capability. Objective intent must be manifested through concrete business plans, market feasibility studies, commercialization budgets, and contractual structures that preserve the taxpayer's right to exploit the technology. Practical capability must be demonstrated by retaining sufficient working capital, technical personnel, industry expertise, or committed financing channels necessary to manufacture, market, or actively license the resulting products. Green itself did not apply this two-prong test; rather, the Court relied on the amended limited partnership agreement and the Confidential Private Offering Memorandum to find that the four inventions were the only inventions in which LaSala would invest, and on the exclusiveness of NPDC's license to find that LaSala itself would never be able to produce or market them (83 T.C. at 688–689).
Surrender of Contractual Direction and Technical Control Over R&D Execution

The third major evidentiary failure identified by the Tax Court in Green was the partnership's total lack of contractual and operational control over the R&D process itself. Under the R&D Agreements executed between LaSala and NPDC, NPDC undertook only to extend its best efforts, within the resources provided, to accomplish the development objectives; all product development was at LaSala's risk, NPDC disclaimed any warranty that a commercially viable product would result, and the services were to terminate by October 1, 1981, whether or not development was complete (83 T.C. at 672). The R&D agreements gave LaSala no power to supervise, review, or direct NPDC's activities: LaSala was entitled only to quarterly progress reports and to confer with NPDC's representatives about them, and its sole remedy for a breach was to terminate the agreement and sue for breach of contract (83 T.C. at 672, 682–683).

When the petitioners relied on an affidavit of Mr. Pinsky, president of the general partner, attesting that he received and reviewed NPDC's progress reports and met with NPDC to discuss its development activities, the Tax Court held that this did not mean LaSala had the power to control those activities, and that even an active role in directing the research would not place LaSala in a trade or business, because any income from the developed inventions would arise from the business of NPDC, the owner of all rights in the inventions; the Court therefore concluded that the extent of LaSala's supervision, if any, was not material (83 T.C. at 682–683, 690, citing Whipple v. Commissioner, 373 U.S. 193 (1963)). The Seventh Circuit later adopted a Tax Court opinion stating that, in the absence of a contractual right to control a contractor's services, the extent of supervision over such services is not material (Goulding, 928 F.2d 1135). The Court described LaSala's 1979 activities as very limited and its activities in later years as purely ministerial (maintaining a partnership bank account, depositing the limited partners' installments, paying the inventors' recourse installments, the general partner's management fee, and legal and accounting fees, and having Tower Hill employees meet with NPDC about its progress), held that the management of investments is not a trade or business, and likened LaSala's royalty interest to that of an investor in securities (83 T.C. at 688–689).
The Anti-Attribution Principle: Misapplication of Treasury Regulation § 1.174-2(a)

A subtle yet critical legal failure in Green involved the petitioner's misinterpretation of Treasury Regulation § 1.174-2(a)(2) (now § 1.174-2(a)(10)), which permits a taxpayer to deduct costs for research "carried on in his behalf by another person or organization". The petitioners argued that LaSala's interest in future royalties was sufficient in itself to mean that NPDC conducted the development activities on LaSala's behalf, and relied on Cleveland v. Commissioner, 297 F.2d 169 (4th Cir. 1961), in which an inventor's research conducted on behalf of a joint venture was attributed to that joint venture (83 T.C. at 685, 690–691).

The Tax Court distinguished Cleveland because the joint venture there owned the inventions and the combined activities of both participants formed the trade or business, whereas LaSala had sold to NPDC all its rights to any product resulting from the research and was not engaged in the business of developing the product; having found that the expenditures were not incurred in connection with a trade or business, the Court expressly found it unnecessary to decide whether the research was conducted on LaSala's behalf under Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(a)(2) (83 T.C. at 691). Subsequent appellate rulings, notably Harris v. Commissioner, 16 F.3d 75 (5th Cir. 1994), articulated what tax practitioners refer to as the Anti-Attribution Principle: although Treasury Regulation § 1.174-2(a)(2) permits an outside contractor to perform research on behalf of the taxpayer, it does not permit the outside contractor to conduct a trade or business on behalf of the taxpayer. Relying on the Supreme Court's landmark decision in Whipple v. Commissioner, 373 U.S. 193 (1963), the Tax Court underscored that federal tax law draws a fundamental, non-negotiable distinction between engaging in a business of one's own and investing in the business of another entity. Under this later line of authority, for contract research to be conducted "on behalf of" a taxpayer under IRC § 174, the research results must be destined for deployment in the taxpayer's own existing or prospective trade or business, not the trade or business of the research contractor.
Cascading Disqualification Under IRC § 41: Carrying On a Business, Contract Research, and Substantial Rights

While Green v. Commissioner adjudicated an IRC § 174 deduction claimed for the 1979 tax year (two years prior to the enactment of the research credit in 1981) and did not address the credit, its reasoning carries over to contemporary R&D tax credit claims under IRC § 41 because IRC § 41 incorporates the IRC § 174 requirements. In modern IRS examinations, a Green-type structural defect can trigger four simultaneous disqualifications under IRC § 41.

First, the arrangement fails the threshold Section 174 Eligibility Test under IRC § 41(d)(1)(A), which mandates that research cannot qualify as "qualified research" unless the underlying expenditures may be treated as specified research or experimental expenditures under IRC § 174. Because a Green-deficient entity fails the "in connection with a trade or business" requirement of IRC § 174, 100% of its claimed QREs automatically fail the first prong of the four-part test under IRC § 41(d).

Second, the structure fails the heightened "carrying on" nexus of IRC § 41(b)(1) and the limits of the start-up exception under IRC § 41(b)(4). Unlike IRC § 174, which uses the broader phrase "in connection with" a trade or business, IRC § 41(b)(1) restricts QREs to amounts paid or incurred "in carrying on any trade or business of the taxpayer" (mirroring IRC § 162). This requires the taxpayer to be actively operating a trade or business at the exact time the QREs are incurred. Furthermore, while Congress enacted a narrow start-up exception in IRC § 41(b)(4)—treating a taxpayer as meeting the "carrying on" test if, at the time the expenses are paid or incurred, the principal purpose of the taxpayer in making the expenditures is to use the results of the research in the active conduct of a future trade or business—this statutory exception applies exclusively to in-house research expenses. Contract research expenses paid by a pre-operational entity that is not yet "carrying on" an active trade or business are statutorily barred from IRC § 41 eligibility, and even in-house expenses fail IRC § 41(b)(4) if the taxpayer lacks a realistic prospect of active conduct under the line of authority that developed from Green.

Third, pre-wired exclusive licensing invalidates contract research "on behalf of" status under IRC § 41(b)(3) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(e)(1)–(3). A taxpayer may claim 65% of amounts paid to a third party for qualified research only if the agreement is entered into prior to the performance of the research, provides that the research be performed "on behalf of" the taxpayer, and requires the taxpayer to bear the expense even if the research is unsuccessful. Under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(e)(3), qualified research is performed "on behalf of" the taxpayer only if the taxpayer has a right to the research results. Where a taxpayer simultaneously grants an exclusive worldwide license to the research contractor (as LaSala did with NPDC, although Green itself did not decide the "on behalf of" question), the contractor—not the taxpayer—holds the beneficial right to the research results, invalidating the contract research expense.

Fourth, the transaction triggers the "funded research" and "substantial rights" exclusions under IRC § 41(d)(4)(H) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d). Under IRC § 41(d)(4)(H), qualified research excludes any research to the extent funded by any grant, contract, or otherwise by another person. Under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d)(2) and (3), if a taxpayer performing or claiming research retains "no substantial rights" in the research under the agreement providing for the research, the research is treated as fully funded and zero expenses qualify as QREs. Moreover, Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d)(3)(i) explicitly stipulates that a taxpayer does not retain substantial rights in the research if the taxpayer must pay for the right to use the results of the research, or if the taxpayer is contractually stripped of the right to use the research results in its own trade or business.
3. Comparative Summary Table

The following table maps each statutory and regulatory requirement implicated in Green v. Commissioner and its related IRC § 41 counterparts against the specific factual failures of the taxpayer (LaSala) and the evidentiary standard of proof established by the Tax Court and federal appellate courts.

headers: Taxpayer's Specific Failure in Green v. Commissioner
The Court's Standard of Proof & Evidentiary Mandate

cells: Trade or Business Nexus (IRC § 174(a)(1); IRC § 174A; Snow v. Commissioner, 416 U.S. 500)
Research and experimental expenditures must be paid or incurred "in connection with" the taxpayer's own existing or prospective trade or business.

Petitioners argued that, under Snow and Cleveland, LaSala's role in the development of the inventions sufficed to place its R&D payments "in connection with" a trade or business, even though LaSala had sold all rights in the inventions to NPDC and its activities never surpassed those of an investor.

Substantial and Regular Activity Standard: Taxpayer must prove through objective facts and circumstances that it will be engaged in a trade or business at some time, and that its activities are sufficiently substantial and regular to constitute a business rather than a passive investment.
Realistic Prospect of Entering Business (IRC § 174(a)(1); cf. Green, 83 T.C. at 686–689; Spellman, 845 F.2d 148; Harris, 16 F.3d 75; Kantor, 998 F.2d 1514)
A pre-operational taxpayer must possess a "realistic prospect" (probability, not mere legal possibility) of utilizing the fruits of the R&D in a business of its own.

Because of NPDC's exclusive license, LaSala itself would never be able to produce or market the inventions; its entire projected capital of $1,376,000 was to be spent within 25 months on R&D fees ($650,000), invention acquisition installments, and management, organization, legal, accounting, and offeree representative fees.

Conjunctive Intent & Capability Test (developed in post-Green appellate decisions): Taxpayer bears the burden of proving both (1) objective intent (business plans, market preparation) and (2) practical capability (capital reserves, personnel, technical expertise, and unencumbered rights) to commercialize the technology itself.
Retention of Ownership & Substantial Rights (IRC § 174(a); IRC § 41(d)(4)(H); Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d)(2)–(3))
Taxpayer must retain beneficial ownership and "substantial rights" to exploit the developed IP in its own business, rather than selling all rights at inception.

Simultaneously with acquiring four inventions and contracting for R&D, LaSala granted NPDC an immediately effective, worldwide exclusive license for the life of the patents, which the Court held to be a same-day sale.

Substance Over Form / Economic Reality Test: Whether a transfer is a sale or a license depends on the legal effect of its provisions, not the name the agreement gives itself (Waterman v. MacKenzie, 138 U.S. 252; 83 T.C. at 679). Retaining only a passive royalty stream after granting a lifetime worldwide exclusive license fails to preserve business ownership or substantial rights.
Licensing as an Active Trade or Business (IRC §§ 162, 174; Green, 83 T.C. at 689–690; Avery v. Commissioner, 47 B.T.A. 538 (1942))
Exploiting inventions through regular licenses and sales may constitute a trade or business; a single, prearranged sale does not.
LaSala engaged in a single, pre-wired transaction disposing of all four inventions on day one to a single counterparty (NPDC), leaving no future inventions to license or market.

Continuity and Regularity Mandate: A partnership organized to dispose of a single property in an isolated sale, without making substantial improvements to the property between its acquisition and sale, is not in the business of selling property of that kind (83 T.C. at 689–690); later practice looks for a continuous pattern of developing technologies, marketing IP to multiple licensees, and negotiating licensing terms after development.
Contractual Direction & Technical Control Over R&D (Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(a)(10); Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(e); Green, 83 T.C. at 690)
When research is outsourced, the taxpayer must retain contractual authority to direct the scope, specifications, and governance of the research performed "on its behalf".

The R&D agreements gave LaSala no power to supervise, review, or direct NPDC's activities (only quarterly progress reports and conferences, with termination and suit as its sole remedy); LaSala's activities were purely ministerial.

Enforceable Contractual Control Standard: In Green, receiving and reviewing progress reports and meeting with the contractor did not establish a power to control, and because LaSala had sold all rights to NPDC, even an active role in directing the research would not have made it a trade or business (83 T.C. at 682–683, 690); Goulding later treated supervision as immaterial absent a contractual right to control. Taxpayer must prove enforceable contractual rights to direct, approve, modify, or terminate technical R&D phases.
Anti-Attribution of Contractor's Business (Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(a)(2)/(10); Whipple, 373 U.S. 193; Harris, 16 F.3d 75)
While a contractor may perform research on behalf of the taxpayer, the contractor's trade or business cannot be attributed to the taxpayer.

Petitioners relied on Cleveland v. Commissioner, 297 F.2d 169, where an inventor's research was attributed to a joint venture, and argued that LaSala's royalty interest meant NPDC developed the inventions on LaSala's behalf; the Court distinguished Cleveland and did not reach the "on behalf of" question.

Independent Entity Attribution Bar: Taxpayer must prove that the prospective business is its own distinct enterprise and not that of the research contractor or licensee; agency attribution of trade or business status is rejected absent true joint venture operational control.
Active "Carrying On" & Start-Up QRE Rules (IRC § 41(b)(1); IRC § 41(b)(4); IRC § 41(b)(2)(B))
For the R&D credit, QREs must be incurred "in carrying on" an active business; start-up exception (§ 41(b)(4)) covers only in-house QREs where principal purpose is active future business conduct.

Not at issue in Green, whose 1979 deduction predates the 1981 enactment of the credit; by analogy, a pre-operational passive syndicate incurring 100% contract research expenses has no active business under § 41(b)(1) and is statutorily ineligible for the § 41(b)(4) in-house start-up safe harbor.

Contemporaneous Operational & Nexus Substantiation: Taxpayer must prove active ongoing business operations (or common control aggregation under § 41(f)(1)) at the time contract QREs are incurred, plus contemporaneous project-level documentation of the process of experimentation.

body.text: 4. Two Applied Remedial Case Studies

To translate the doctrinal mandates of Green v. Commissioner and its statutory counterparts in IRC §§ 174 and 41 into actionable tax planning, the following two applied industry case studies examine realistic commercial ventures facing the exact legal, contractual, and evidentiary pitfalls that caused disqualification in Green. Each case study demonstrates step-by-step how the taxpayer can restructure project governance, contractual terms, intellectual property retention, and technical experimentation tracking to overcome judicial scrutiny and establish full statutory compliance.
Case Study 1: Biopharmaceutical Special Purpose Vehicle (SPV) & Contract Research Organization (CRO) Co-Development
Baseline Vulnerability Profile: The Pre-Wired Licensing Trap

OncoVanguard Partners LP ("OncoVanguard"), a newly formed Delaware limited partnership backed by high-net-worth life sciences investors and a venture capital general partner, raises $25 million in committed capital. OncoVanguard's stated purpose is to acquire four preclinical small-molecule kinase inhibitor compounds from university technology transfer offices, fund preclinical toxicology and Phase I/IIa clinical formulation R&D, and monetize the resulting drug candidates. Because OncoVanguard employs no laboratory scientists and owns no wet-lab facilities, it simultaneously executes two agreements on December 15 with Apex BioPharma Corp. ("Apex"), an established pharmaceutical manufacturer.

Under the Master Development Agreement (MDA), OncoVanguard commits $22 million of its $25 million capital to Apex to conduct all formulation engineering, stability testing, and Phase I/IIa clinical trials, while Section 14 of the MDA stipulates that Apex is an independent contractor maintaining sole and exclusive control over all scientific personnel, laboratory protocols, and experimental methods. Simultaneously, under a Commercialization & Exclusive License Agreement (CELA) executed on the same day, OncoVanguard grants Apex an immediate, worldwide exclusive license to manufacture, market, and distribute all four kinase inhibitor compounds for the duration of their patent terms in exchange for a 6% royalty on net commercial sales (or, alternatively, grants Apex an exclusive option exercisable at any time for a nominal fee of $50,000).

Under Green v. Commissioner—and directly analogous R&D partnership rulings such as Spellman v. Commissioner, 845 F.2d 148, and LDL Research & Development II, Ltd. v. Commissioner, 124 F.3d 1338—the IRS will disallow 100% of OncoVanguard's IRC § 174 deductions and any claimed IRC § 41 R&D tax credits. By simultaneously granting Apex a worldwide exclusive license (or nominal-fee option) while committing 88% of its capital to R&D fees and surrendering all technical control under Section 14 of the MDA, OncoVanguard has effected an immediate sale of the four compounds to Apex and functions solely as a passive investor in Apex's pharmaceutical business. Furthermore, because OncoVanguard is a pre-operational entity with zero in-house wages and 100% contract research expenses, it fails the "carrying on any trade or business" requirement of IRC § 41(b)(1) and cannot utilize the IRC § 41(b)(4) start-up safe harbor.
Step 1: Project Governance and Operational Substance Restructuring

To establish both an active licensing or development trade or business and a "realistic prospect" of independent commercialization under Green, OncoVanguard must dismantle its passive syndicate structure and establish genuine operational capability prior to incurring R&D expenses. Rather than operating as an empty shell with zero employees, OncoVanguard must directly employ a Chief Medical Officer (CMO), a Vice President of Pharmaceutical Chemistry, and Senior Clinical Project Managers on its W-2 payroll. These internal scientific executives must actively design the overarching clinical development strategy, author target product profiles (TPPs), and perform direct supervision and direct support of the research under IRC § 41(b)(2)(B).

To institutionalize technical control, OncoVanguard must establish a formal Joint Steering Committee (JSC) governed by a written charter requiring bi-weekly technical review meetings—analogous to the "Science Meetings" validated by the IRS Office of Chief Counsel in Field Attorney Advice (FAA) 20055203F. Under the JSC charter, OncoVanguard's appointed scientific executives must hold affirmative tie-breaking vote and veto authority over all material R&D decisions, including dosage formulation modifications, toxicology protocol amendments, synthesis pathway selections, and clinical go/no-go stage gates. Simultaneously, OncoVanguard must restructure its $25 million capital allocation so that no more than 60% ($15 million) is committed to initial contract R&D, while $10 million (supplemented by committed institutional credit lines or reserved venture tranches) is explicitly ring-fenced in escrow for post-Phase II independent commercialization, co-promotion, or multi-party licensing operations.
Step 2: Contractual and Intellectual Property Restructuring

OncoVanguard must sever the simultaneous pre-wired licensing tie with Apex and rewrite the MDA to comply with Green, Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(a)(10), Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(e), and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d). First, the CELA must be eliminated in its entirety prior to the commencement of R&D. Apex must be engaged strictly as a fee-for-service Contract Research Organization (CRO) under the MDA, with zero pre-existing options, rights of first refusal, or exclusive licenses to commercialize the four compounds. The MDA must explicitly stipulate that 100% of all foreground and background improvements, synthesis processes, clinical trial data, Investigational New Drug (IND) filings, and patent rights vest solely and exclusively in OncoVanguard upon creation, thereby satisfying both the "on behalf of" requirement of Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(e)(3) and the "substantial rights" mandate of Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d)(2).

Second, Section 14 of the MDA must be redrafted to excise all boilerplate independent-contractor language stating that OncoVanguard is "interested only in the results obtained". In its place, the contract must grant OncoVanguard the enforceable legal right to direct technical specifications, audit laboratory notebooks in real time, reassign synthesis tasks among multiple competing CROs, and terminate work orders at any technical milestone. To satisfy the financial risk requirement of Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(e)(2)(iii), the MDA must structure payments on a time-and-materials or non-refundable technical milestone basis where OncoVanguard bears 100% of the financial risk of scientific failure, obligating OncoVanguard to pay Apex for research services performed regardless of whether the kinase inhibitors achieve clinical efficacy.

Third, to qualify as an active licensing trade or business under Green, Avery v. Commissioner, 47 B.T.A. 538 (1942), and IRS FAA 20055203F, OncoVanguard must utilize an internal business development team to market the post-Phase II compounds across the global pharmaceutical industry, granting territorial or indication-specific licenses to multiple counterparties at fair-market valuations negotiated after technical uncertainty is resolved, while retaining U.S. co-promotion rights. Furthermore, because IRC § 41(b)(4) only permits pre-operational taxpayers to claim in-house QREs, OncoVanguard can ensure its 65% contract research QREs qualify under IRC § 41(b)(1) by either acquiring an existing revenue-generating diagnostic or specialty reagent business line so that it is actively "carrying on" a trade or business during the tax year, or structuring the venture as a majority-owned (>50%) subsidiary of an operating pharmaceutical parent corporation to invoke the controlled group aggregation rules of IRC § 41(f)(1), thereby attributing the active trade or business status of the controlled group to OncoVanguard.
Step 3: Technical Documentation and Experimentation Tracking

To withstand IRS examination under the strict substantiation standards of IRC § 6001 and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(d), OncoVanguard must implement a contemporaneous, project-by-project documentation protocol linking its internal scientific direction to the CRO's experimental execution. Each of the four kinase inhibitor compounds must be tracked as a distinct "business component" under IRC § 41(d)(2)(A), with segregated general ledger cost centers and project accounting codes.

For each compound, OncoVanguard's CMO and VP of Chemistry must maintain dated Technical Uncertainty and Hypothesis Ledgers documenting the specific pharmacokinetic, bioavailability, or metabolic toxicity uncertainties that could not be resolved through standard scientific knowledge at the outset of each preclinical and clinical phase. Every bi-weekly JSC meeting minute must contemporaneously record the specific alternative molecular formulations tested by Apex, quantitative assay results, failed synthesis batches, and OncoVanguard's written technical directives modifying the next iteration of experiments. Finally, OncoVanguard's W-2 scientific staff must maintain weekly contemporaneous time logs allocating their hours by specific compound and activity type (distinguishing direct supervision of bioavailability assays from non-qualifying investor relations), while Apex must submit itemized monthly invoices breaking down labor hours and consumable laboratory supplies by specific experimental protocol, explicitly excluding non-qualifying costs such as patent prosecution fees, market research, or routine quality control testing under Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(a)(3).
Case Study 2: Industrial Clean-Tech & Aerospace Propulsion Joint Venture Utilizing Outsourced Engineering
Baseline Vulnerability Profile: The Turnkey Contractor & Royalty Clawback Trap

AeroHydro Dynamics LLC ("AeroHydro"), taxed as a partnership for federal income tax purposes, is formed by a syndicate of aviation leasing executives and private equity investors to fund the development of a novel liquid-hydrogen cryogenic fuel injection system and superconducting electric turbine for regional commercial aircraft. AeroHydro acquires initial conceptual computer-aided design (CAD) schematics from an independent aerospace engineer and immediately enters into a Turnkey Engineering & Commercialization Agreement (TECA) with Titan Aerospace Corp. ("Titan"), a Tier-1 aerospace original equipment manufacturer (OEM).

Under the TECA, AeroHydro agrees to pay Titan a fixed turnkey fee of $18 million over two years to design, simulate, fabricate, and wind-tunnel test three full-scale prototype propulsion units. In the same agreement, Titan is granted the exclusive global right to manufacture, integrate, and sell the resulting propulsion systems to commercial airframe manufacturers for 20 years, paying AeroHydro a passive royalty of $35,000 per turbine unit sold. Additionally, to protect Titan's proprietary manufacturing methods, the TECA stipulates that Titan retains legal title to all manufacturing tooling, wind-tunnel test rigs, and process improvements developed during the research program, while AeroHydro holds nominal title only to the baseline conceptual patent. Finally, the contract specifies that if AeroHydro wishes to utilize the resulting propulsion designs or metallurgical data for non-aviation applications (such as marine propulsion or stationary power generation), AeroHydro must pay Titan a licensing fee equal to 10% of gross revenues.

This arrangement triggers comprehensive disqualification under Green v. Commissioner, Zink v. United States (929 F.2d 1015, disallowing deductions for outsourced aircraft component R&D where investors lacked capability to manufacture or market aircraft components), and Harris v. Commissioner (16 F.3d 75, disallowing deductions where the research contractor held exclusive sublicensing rights). First, under IRC § 174, AeroHydro has no realistic prospect of entering the aerospace manufacturing or licensing business because Titan holds the exclusive 20-year right to manufacture and sell the turbines and owns all process improvements. Second, under Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(a)(2)/(10) and Harris, Titan's active aerospace trade or business cannot be attributed to AeroHydro. Third, under IRC § 41(d)(4)(H) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d)(3)(i), because AeroHydro must pay Titan a 10% royalty to use the research results in non-aviation fields and relinquished all aviation commercialization rights to Titan, AeroHydro retains no substantial rights in the research. Fourth, because the $18 million payment is structured as a fixed-fee turnkey deliverable guaranteed to produce working prototypes, the IRS can recharacterize the payment under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(e)(2) as a non-qualifying payment for "the product or result" of the research contingent on success, rather than qualified contract research.
Step 1: Project Governance and Active Trade or Business Integration

To overcome the judicial barriers of Green, Zink, and Harris, AeroHydro must transform from a passive financing syndicate into an active aerospace propulsion manufacturer and multi-field technology licensor. Instead of operating as a passive investment vehicle, AeroHydro must lease a dedicated propulsion assembly and cryo-testing facility, hire an in-house W-2 engineering team comprising a Chief Technology Officer (CTO), cryogenic fluid dynamicists, and aerospace metallurgists, and actively fabricate and assemble the cryogenic fuel-delivery sub-assemblies in-house, utilizing Titan strictly as a specialized subcontractor for high-altitude wind-tunnel testing and precision turbine blade casting.

AeroHydro's CTO and internal engineering leads must author the Master System Requirements Document (SRD), establish quantitative thermal efficiency and thrust-to-weight performance thresholds, and actively direct Titan's engineering personnel through mandatory weekly Engineering Design Reviews (EDRs). On the commercial front, AeroHydro must establish internal commercial sales and business development operations to market and sell the integrated propulsion systems directly to regional airframe OEMs, engaging Titan solely on a non-exclusive contract manufacturing (tolling) basis where AeroHydro owns the work-in-process and finished inventory, establishes customer pricing, bears commercial warranty risk, and recognizes gross receipts directly from airframe customers.
Step 2: Contractual and Intellectual Property Restructuring

The single Turnkey Engineering & Commercialization Agreement between AeroHydro and Titan must be rescinded and replaced with two separate, arm's-length commercial contracts executed at distinct stages of the product lifecycle: an upfront Master Research & Engineering Services Agreement (MRESA) and a subsequent, independent Non-Exclusive Contract Manufacturing Agreement (NECMA) negotiated only after prototype validation. All contractual provisions granting Titan exclusive global manufacturing, marketing, or sales rights—as well as all provisions converting AeroHydro's ownership interest into a per-unit royalty—must be eliminated. Under the subsequent NECMA, Titan functions strictly as a toll manufacturer producing turbine components to AeroHydro's specifications for a negotiated per-unit fabrication fee, while AeroHydro retains 100% of worldwide commercial sales and distribution rights.

Under the MRESA, 100% of legal and equitable title to all foreground inventions, CAD models, computational fluid dynamics (CFD) simulation code, metallurgical process improvements, specialized tooling designs, and prototype hardware must vest unconditionally in AeroHydro immediately upon creation. Crucially, the clause requiring AeroHydro to pay Titan a 10% licensing fee to use the research results in marine or stationary power applications must be deleted in its entirety, ensuring strict compliance with Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d)(3)(i), which dictates that a taxpayer does not retain substantial rights in research if the taxpayer must pay for the right to use the research results. Furthermore, to ensure AeroHydro qualifies for the 65% contract research credit under IRC § 41(b)(3) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(e)(2), the MRESA must replace the fixed-price turnkey deliverable structure with a time-and-materials engineering rate schedule. The MRESA must explicitly obligate AeroHydro to pay Titan for all engineering hours and wind-tunnel test runs performed in accordance with AeroHydro's technical directives, regardless of whether the prototype propulsion system successfully achieves target cryogenic combustion stability.
Step 3: Technical Documentation and Experimentation Tracking

To satisfy the stringent pilot model and process-of-experimentation substantiation rules under IRC §§ 174 and 41—and to avoid the evidentiary disallowances sustained in cases such as Betz v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2023-84, and Little Sandy Coal Co. v. Commissioner, 62 F.4th 287 (7th Cir. 2023)—AeroHydro must institute rigorous engineering documentation protocols. The three full-scale prototype propulsion units must be contemporaneously documented as "pilot models" under Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(a)(4), specifically establishing that AeroHydro faced fundamental engineering uncertainty regarding the integrated cryogenic turbine architecture, that the prototypes were constructed solely to resolve those design uncertainties through destructive and operational wind-tunnel testing, and that the test units will not be sold or placed into commercial fleet service.

AeroHydro's in-house engineers must maintain an integrated Product Lifecycle Management (PLM) and CAD version-control repository directly linked to Titan's test cell telemetry. For each distinct sub-component business component (such as the cryogenic fuel injector nozzle, the superconducting stator winding, and the thermal barrier coating), the PLM archive must contemporaneously record the baseline technical uncertainty (such as hydrogen embrittlement and two-phase cavitation at cryogenic liquid-hydrogen temperatures under high-pressure injection), the specific design alternatives modeled via Finite Element Analysis (FEA) and CFD simulations, quantitative test cell data capturing pressure drops and thermal gradients across iterative test runs, and formal Engineering Change Orders (ECOs) signed by AeroHydro's CTO directing Titan to modify nozzle geometry for subsequent experimental iterations. Finally, AeroHydro's accounting system must segregate the costs of raw alloys and liquid hydrogen consumed directly in wind-tunnel testing (eligible as supply QREs under IRC § 41(b)(2)(A)(ii)) from general capital equipment and depreciable test facilities (excluded under IRC § 174(c) and § 41(b)(2)(C)), while matching every contractor engineering hour billed by Titan to a specific, dated ECO and experimental test protocol.
Summary Matrix of Applied Remedial Restructuring Across Case Studies

cells: Entity Governance & Personnel
Passive limited partnership or LLC that conducts no research itself; purely ministerial administration.
Active operating company or controlled group member employing W-2 technical executives (CMO/CTO) exercising JSC veto power and direct supervision.
IRC §§ 174(a), 41(b)(1), 41(b)(2)(B), 41(f)(1); Green, 83 T.C. 667; IRS FAA 20055203F.
IP Ownership & Licensing Timing
Simultaneous day-one execution of R&D contract and worldwide exclusive license (or nominal option) to contractor.
Unencumbered 100% IP vesting in taxpayer; zero pre-wired contractor licenses; post-R&D multi-party licensing or direct product commercialization.
Royalty / Usage Restrictions
Taxpayer relegated to passive royalty stream or required to pay contractor a fee to use research in other fields.
Taxpayer holds royalty-free, unrestricted global exploitation rights across all fields of use; contractor paid solely for R&D or toll manufacturing services.
Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d)(3)(i); Green, 83 T.C. at 689; Harris, 16 F.3d 75.
Contractual Control & Risk Allocation
Taxpayer holds no contractual power to supervise, review, or direct the contractor's research (as in Green), or pays a turnkey fixed-result fee.
Taxpayer retains enforceable contractual control over specifications, stage-gates, and ECOs; time-and-materials payment bearing full risk of failure.
Working Capital & Commercial Capability

All raised capital committed upfront (in Green, the entire $1,376,000 was projected to be spent within 25 months on R&D, acquisition installments, and management, organization, legal, accounting, and offeree representative fees); no reserves for manufacturing or marketing.
Dedicated working capital reserves, credit facilities, and business development budgets sufficient to fund post-R&D manufacturing or licensing.
Green, 83 T.C. at 669, 687–688; Kantor, 998 F.2d at 1520; Zink, 929 F.2d 1015.
Technical & Financial Substantiation
High-level summary progress reports and lump-sum contractor invoices lacking nexus to specific business components.
Contemporaneous PLM/clinical hypothesis logs, JSC minutes, ECOs, pilot model trackers, and itemized time/supply invoices mapped by business component.

body.text: 5. Strategic Synthesis for Federal Tax Practitioners

More than four decades after its promulgation by the United States Tax Court, Green v. Commissioner, 83 T.C. 667 (1984), remains the premier analytical filter through which the Internal Revenue Service and the federal judiciary evaluate multi-party research arrangements, joint ventures, and special purpose vehicles. The enduring lesson of Green is that the statutory liberality of Snow v. Commissioner—which opened IRC § 174 to pre-operational start-up businesses—cannot be weaponized to transform passive capital providers into research-conducting businesses through formalistic contract labels.

For tax attorneys and technical advisors structuring contemporary R&D transactions under IRC §§ 174, 174A, and 41, audit readiness requires aligning commercial reality, contractual drafting, and technical governance prior to the execution of any research agreement. First, the entity claiming the research deductions or credits must possess both the objective intent and the unencumbered financial and operational capability to deploy the resulting intellectual property in its own active trade or business—whether through direct manufacturing and sales or through a continuous, multi-counterparty licensing enterprise. Second, tax counsel must rigorously vet all ancillary agreements—including side letters, joint venture operating agreements, purchase options, and commercialization licenses—to ensure the taxpayer does not simultaneously grant an exclusive license or low-cost buyout option to the research contractor before the research is completed. An upfront grant to the contractor of the exclusive right to make, use, and sell the invention for the life of the patent will be treated as a sale under Green, leaving the taxpayer with only an investor-like royalty interest, and will jeopardize "substantial rights" and "on behalf of" eligibility under IRC § 41. Finally, because the Tax Court in Green treated the extent of LaSala's actual supervision as immaterial where the R&D agreements conferred no power to supervise, review, or direct the contractor and LaSala had sold all rights in the inventions, research agreements must explicitly codify the taxpayer's authority to direct technical specifications, approve experimental iterations, and bear the financial risk of failure, backed by contemporaneous, project-level documentation linking internal scientific supervision to every dollar of claimed Qualified Research Expenses.

metaDescription: Green v. Commissioner, 83 T.C. 667 (1984): R&D costs qualify under IRC § 174 only if incurred in connection with the taxpayer's own trade or business.
